definitions.definition: A perfected one: in Tamil, cittar — the yogin-poets, physicians and alchemists who have attained the powers (citti) and the deathless state, and who stand outside caste and temple ritual.

Tamil citti: the powers won by yoga and kāya-citti — above all the eight great powers (aṭṭamā citti) of the Tirumantiram; Kaṭuveḷi says they come to anyone only by Śiva's action, and Tāyumāṉavar holds them easier than stilling the mind.

The breath treated as a horse to be mastered: the Siddhar breath-yoga (vāci yōkam) that stills and turns the breath inward and is held to perfect the body and lengthen life (summary; see prc:vasi-yoga).

equivalents.note: vāci is the breath as the object of mastery

definitions.definition: The root: the lowest support (mūlātāram) where the fire and the goddess Vālai are placed; in the Tirumūla ñāṉam also the letter 'a' as the ground of all. 'To know that root is liberation' (Kaṭuveḷi 13).
The six supports (āṟu ātāram) of the body: mūlātāram, cuvātiṭṭāṉam, maṇipūrakam, anākatam, vicutti, ākkiñai; the Siddha counterpart of the cakras, burnt away by the guru's grace in Aḻukaṇṇi's song.

equivalents.note: the six ātāras correspond to the six cakras

definitions.definition: The open, empty space — the supreme as boundless void-expanse beyond the crown; 'for those who hold the open space to be the truth, what need of a title-deed?' (Kuṭampai 1); Kaṭuveḷi speaks of 'the open space of pure Vedānta'.

equivalents.note: space as image of the supreme
the Siddhar 'void' is not the Buddhist emptiness; resemblance only

definitions.definition: The Supreme beyond the supreme; Tāyumāṉavar's address to the ultimate in the refrain of the Paraparakkaṇṇi.
Light, flame: the Lord seen as light within ('the light mingled within', Sivavākkiyar; 'like the inner light of a ruby', Aḻukaṇṇi; 'the supreme light' parañcōti).
For the Siddhars, Civam is the supreme within the body, identical with love ('love is Civam', TM 270) and reached by inner knowledge rather than temple ritual.
Love, which the Siddhars, after TM 270, identify with Civam itself.
Grace: for the Siddha poets the guru's descent and self-showing (Aḻukaṇṇi 33–34) and the Lord's flood of compassion (Pattirakiriyār 62).
The body (also uṭampu, kāyam, tēkam): for the Siddhars both a leaking pot of filth to be seen through (Aḻukaṇṇi 8; Paṭṭiṉattār) and the Lord's temple to be preserved and perfected (TM 724–725).
The soul (also uyir, 'life'): the player of the body's play; when it leaves, the body withers (Kaṭuveḷi 21).
Desire, pursuit; the 'three desires' (ēṭaṇai mūṉṟu) of the ninety-six principles, called evil by Kaṭuveḷi.
Caste (birth-group), which the Siddhars declare baseless — 'is there a difference in flesh, skin and bone?' (Sivavākkiyar); 'the castes called unequal are one' (Kaṭuveḷi 32).

equivalents.note: Tamil form of jāti (in the social sense)

definitions.definition: The young goddess (Bālā), the Siddhars' Śakti worshipped at the root with three syllables; identified with Maṉōṉmaṇi.
'Jewel of the mind' — the supreme goddess as mother and light in the Siddhar worship; in yoga texts also the name of the state beyond mind (manonmanī).
The letter 'a', ground and root of all letters and of all things; in the Tirumūla ñāṉam the Supreme itself (taṟparam).
The letter 'u', which in the Tirumūla ñāṉam is supreme consciousness (ciṟparam), paired with akāram.
The unspoken mantra: the identity of guru and Lord, He and She, known without utterance (Tirumūla ñāṉam 6).

equivalents.note: both name a mantra not recited aloud; the Tamil verse does not mention the breath

definitions.definition: The noble one, the master-guru whom the seeker must find and bow to (Pattirakiriyār 26).
Rejuvenating preparations and regimens (kāya kaṟpam) — herbal, mineral-metal, breath and yogic — meant to make the body firm and long-lived; dismissed as needless for the true knower by Kuṭampai (2).

equivalents.note: both name rejuvenation; kaṟpam also covers breath and yogic means

definitions.definition: Perfection of the body — the Siddhar goal of an undecaying, powerful body as the vessel of liberation; 'after kāyacitti removed my karma' (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 14).
'Dying without dying': the death of ego and the mortal body while living, by which death is conquered (Aḻukaṇṇi 9; Rāmatēvar 2; Kuṭampai 13).
The ninety-six principles that make up the embodied person in the Siddha tradition (see cpt:ninety-six-tattvas).
Tamil tattuvam: the principles of the embodied person, counted in the Siddha tradition as ninety-six; realization burns them away (Aḻukaṇṇi 36).
The secret 'three salts' of Siddha alchemy, said to be the key to fixing mercury and to the deathless body; its composition is deliberately veiled. Summary only.

notes: Restricted subject (alchemy): no identification or process recorded.

definitions.definition: Alchemy — the art (vātam) of transmuting metals and fixing mercury (iracam), in the Siddhar corpus both an outer art and a figure for perfecting the body. Summary only.

notes: 'vātam' also names the wind humour; the homonym is kept apart (see trm:vata). Restricted subject.

definitions.definition: Mercury, the central substance of Siddha alchemy and of the mineral medicines; recorded as a term only.
Code language: the veiled names the Siddhars gave herbs, minerals, processes and yogic states, so that only the guru's disciple could decode them; glossaries (e.g. Akattiyar paripāṣai) explain some.
A couplet stanza with a recurring refrain, the favourite form of the Siddhar songs (Kuṭampai, Pattirakiriyār, Paraparakkaṇṇi).
Simply being still: the silent guru's instruction 'be still' (cummā iru) and the state of mind at rest that Tāyumāṉavar holds harder than every power.

equivalents.note: stillness of mind, of which outer silence is one form

definitions.definition: Harmony, equal flavour: Tāyumāṉavar's reconciliation of Vedānta and Siddhānta (vētānta cittānta camaracam), later taken up by Vallalar.
'Sleeping without sleeping': the yogic sleep of Śiva-yoga, in which the senses are withdrawn but awareness stays (Pattirakiriyār 1–2).

equivalents.note: both name a sleep-like state with awareness; texts and traditions differ

definitions.definition: Macrocosm and microcosm: the Siddhar principle that what is in the cosmic egg is in the body and what is in the body is in the cosmos.
Living samādhi: the tradition's belief that a Siddhar enters samādhi and is interred alive, remaining present at the shrine; the samādhi places of the eighteen are pilgrimage sites.

notes: Recorded as the tradition's belief; no practice details.

definitions.definition: A term of the Tirumantiram's 'amuri tāraṇai' section, read in the Siddha tradition as a bodily 'nectar' used in rejuvenation; recorded as a term only.

notes: Restricted subject (bodily-substance practice): summary only; interpretation low confidence.

definitions.definition: The coiled power at the root, in whose seat Guha is invoked (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam kāppu); Tamil form of kuṇḍalinī.
The three 'faults' or vital humours — vaḷi (vātam), aḻal (pittam), aiyam (kapam) — whose balance is health and whose excess or deficiency causes disease (Kuṟaḷ 941).

equivalents.note: equal in function to Āyurveda's tridoṣa; the Siddha tradition claims independent origin

definitions.definition: Tamil vaḷi or vātam: the wind humour, first of the three (Kuṟaḷ 941 names the three 'beginning with vaḷi'); built of air and ether; in Siddha pulse-reading the strongest beat.
Tamil aḻal or pittam: the fire humour, second of the three.
Tamil aiyam or kapam: the water-earth humour, third of the three.
In Siddha medicine the three humours (Tamil tōṣam, kuṟṟam) — vātam, pittam, kapam — which with the seven tissues make up the ninety-six principles' 'tōṣam 3'.
In Siddha medicine the seven body-constituents (uṭal tātukkaḷ): cāram, ceṉnīr, ūṉ, koḻuppu, eṉpu, mūḷai, cukkilam/curōṇitam; in pharmacy tātu also names the mineral-metal class of drugs.
Tamil nāṭi means both the channels of the subtle body (ten principal ones in the ninety-six) and the pulse, the chief of the eight examinations, read at the wrist for the three humours.
The eight examinations of Siddha diagnosis: pulse (nāṭi), touch (paricam), tongue (nā), colour (niṟam), voice (moḻi), eyes (viḻi), stool (malam) and urine (mūttiram).
Urine signs: examination of the urine's colour, density, smell, froth and deposit.
The oil-drop sign: a drop of oil on the urine spreading like a snake indicates vātam, like a ring pittam, staying like a pearl kapam.
The six tastes — iṉippu (sweet), puḷippu (sour), uppu (salt), kārppu (pungent), kaippu (bitter), tuvarppu (astringent) — each formed of two elements and acting on the humours.
Medicinal herb; the first of the three classes of Siddha drugs (mūlikai — plants, tātu — minerals and metals, jīvam — animal products).
The dietary and behavioural restrictions to be kept during a course of Siddha treatment, held strictest for mineral-metal medicines.
The vehicle (honey, ghee, juice, decoction) with which a medicine is taken.
Purification: the processing by which toxic minerals, metals and plants are said to be rendered usable; the tradition insists that unpurified substances are poison. Term only; no procedure.
A circle: (1) the three circles of fire, sun and moon among the ninety-six principles; (2) in Siddha medicine a fixed course of treatment (commonly forty or forty-eight days).
The five receptacles among the ninety-six principles (stomach, intestine, rectum, bladder, seminal receptacle).
The eight passions among the ninety-six principles — desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, haughtiness and egoism (list recalled at low confidence).
A calcined (white) preparation of a mineral, metal or shell.

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: A red calcined preparation of a metal or mineral.

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: A lime-like calcined preparation, held very potent.

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: 'Binding': a fixed (solidified) mercury or mineral preparation; also a bandage.

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: Calcination in a pit-fire of measured cakes of dung; the basic process of mineral pharmacy.

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: A pill; in the Siddhar legends also the magic pill that gives flight or invisibility.
A herbal powder.
A decoction.
An electuary (confection) of herbs in sugar, honey or ghee.
A medicated oil, for internal use or external application.
A waxy preparation, often containing mineral ingredients.

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: A 'stone', i.e. a poisonous mineral; the tradition counts 64 (32 natural, 32 prepared).

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: The nine pāṣāṇams from which, the tradition says, Bogar made the Palani image of Murukaṉ.

notes: Metal/mineral preparation: name and the tradition's warnings only (see cpt:parpam-centuram); no process or dose.

definitions.definition: Vital points of the body where life-breath concentrates; injury to them harms or kills and pressure on them heals. The Siddha tradition counts 108 (12 'striking' paṭu varmam and 96 'touching' toṭu varmam) and ascribes the lore to Agastya.

equivalents.note: Āyurveda's 107 marmas: overlapping idea, different counts and uses

definitions.definition: Siddha therapeutic massage and manipulation, practised in several kinds.
In the Siddha ninety-six principles, the ten vital winds (Tamil vāyu, with Tamil names pirāṇaṉ, apāṉaṉ, viyāṉaṉ, utāṉaṉ, camāṉaṉ, nākaṉ, kūrmaṉ, kirukaraṉ, tēvatattaṉ, taṉañcayaṉ).
Tamil kuṇṭali: the coiled power at the root, roused by the guru's grace to pass the six supports (Vināyakar akaval; Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam invocation).
Tamil cuḻumuṉai: the central channel, between iṭakalai and piṅkalai, named in the Siddha invocations and among the ten nāṭis.
Tamil iṭakalai: the left channel (lunar), first of the ten nāṭis of the Siddha ninety-six.
Tamil piṅkalai: the right channel (solar), second of the ten nāṭis of the Siddha ninety-six.

In the Tamil Siddha texts the centres are usually called ātāram (supports), six in number, with the crown-space above them; cakkaram names also the worship-diagram (the Meru of forty-three triangles, Caṭṭaimuṉi 1).
Tamil amirtam: the nectar of immortality; for the Siddhars the inner nectar that knowers drink (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 10) and that flows from the moon in the head.

Tamil mantiram: the Siddhars use seed-syllables (the three letters of Vālai, the five letters) yet ask 'for those who stand in the true tantra, why mantra?' (Kuṭampai 7) and prize the unspoken mantra.
Tamil muttirai: seals of yoga and ritual, declared needless for one who remains awake in awareness (Kuṭampai 6).
Tamil añceḻuttu: the five letters (na-ma-ci-vā-ya); chanting them yields birthless release (Paṭṭiṉattār, Tiruttillai 17).
Tamil kuru, ācāṉ, āriyaṉ: for the Siddhars the guru comes of his own accord, shows his own form and burns the bonds; guru and Lord are one (Tirumūla ñāṉam 6).
Tamil yōkam: the Siddhars teach the eight-limbed yoga of the Tirumantiram and vāci yoga, yet Kuṭampai asks what need of yoga the realized has.
Tamil aṭṭāṅka yōkam: iyamam, niyamam, ātaṉam, pirāṇāyāmam, pirattiyākāram, tāraṇai, tiyāṉam, camāti (TM 552), commended by Kaṭuveḷi (31).
Tamil kollāmai: the Siddhar poets condemn killing and flesh-eating (Paṭṭiṉattār; Pattirakiriyār 14; Kaṭuveḷi 25, 29).
Non-killing, which Pattirakiriyār longs for: regarding living beings as one's own life (14).
Refusing flesh: Paṭṭiṉattār asks what flesh-eaters will do when Yama seizes them (Tiruvēkampamālai 33).
Tamil mauṉam: silence — Pattirakiriyār's 'taking the form of a mute' (19); the silent guru of Tāyumāṉavar.
Tamil patti: 'devotion is the highest thing on earth' (Kaṭuveḷi 18); the Siddhars' devotion is to the Lord within and to the guru, not to temple images.
Tamil Yamaṉ, Namaṉ, Kālaṉ: death, who carries off the sinner (Kaṭuveḷi pallavi) but has no hold on knowers (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 10) or on those who conquered him (Kuṭampai 26).
Tamil antakkaraṇam: the four inner faculties (maṉam, putti, cittam, akaṅkāram) among the ninety-six principles.
Tamil avattai: the five states among the ninety-six principles — cākkiram, coppaṉam, cuḻutti, turiyam, turiyātītam.
Tamil kōcam: the five sheaths among the ninety-six principles.
Tamil kēcari: the Tirumantiram's kēcari yōkam section (third tantra), revered by the Siddhars; restricted, summary only.
The two deeds, good and bad, both binding: the Lord drives us 'by the rope of the two deeds' (Paṭṭiṉattār, Tiruttillai 11); the knower no longer seeks either (Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam 13).
Renunciation: Paṭṭiṉattār ranks the renouncer far above the giver and the renouncer-in-mind higher still (Tiruvēkampamālai 1).
Release, 'the house': Kaṭuveḷi's pun — burn the forest of the senses and you will see the house (14); to know the root is the house of liberation (13).
The 'true path': in the Siddhar songs the path of true knowledge (Kaṭuveḷi speaks of books without caṉmārkkam as not to be sought); later the name of Vallalar's movement.
